entry: 1985 Soviet anti-war film directed by Elem Klimov. It is set during the German occupation of Byelorussia in World War II and follows a young Belarusian teenager, Flyora, who joins a partisan unit. The film depicts Nazi atrocities and human suffering inflicted on the populace, mixing hyper-realism with underlying [[Surrealism|surrealism]] and philosophical [[Existentialism|existentialism]]. Klimov had to fight eight years of Soviet censorship before he was allowed to produce the film in its entirety. It received the FIPRESCI prize at the 14th Moscow International Film Festival and was ranked 41st in the 2022 Sight & Sound directors' poll.

Genre of dramatic works intended to be humorous or amusing by inducing laughter.

Comedy originated in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], where [[Satire|political satire]] by comic poets influenced voters in Athenian democracy. Greek comedy typically pitted two groups, ages, genders or societies against each other in an amusing conflict. [[Aristotle]] defined it as an imitation of people worse than the average, and the word derives from *kōmōidía*, a compound of *kômos* (revel) and *ōidḗ* (singing, ode).

Satire and political satire portray people or institutions as ridiculous or corrupt, while [[Parody]] subverts popular genres. Other varieties include screwball, black and romantic comedy, and the comedy of manners, which satirizes upper-class society. In the Middle Ages the term expanded to include narrative poems with happy endings.

Long-period [[Comet|comet]], one of the most widely observed of the 20th century.

Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp discovered it independently on July 23, 1995, before it became visible to the naked eye. It passed perihelion on April 1, 1997, at about magnitude −1.8. Its massive nucleus kept it visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months, twice as long as the Great Comet of 1811, so it was dubbed the Great Comet of 1997. Hale had been tracking comets from his driveway in New Mexico, while Bopp observed through a friend's homemade telescope in Arizona.

Fragmented [[Comet|comet]] that collided with [[Jupiter]] in July 1994.

Carolyn and Eugene M. Shoemaker and David Levy discovered it on March 24, 1993. It was the first active comet observed orbiting a planet, and it had probably been captured by Jupiter 20 to 30 years earlier. In July 1992 it passed within Jupiter's [[Roche limit]], and tidal forces broke it into fragments up to 2 km in diameter. The fragments struck Jupiter's southern hemisphere between July 16 and 22, 1994, at a speed of approximately 60 km/s. The impact scars were more visible than the [[Great Red Spot]] and persisted for many months.

Women and girls forced into sexual slavery by the Imperial Japanese Armed Forces in occupied territories before and during [[World War II]].

The term translates the Japanese *ianfu* (慰安婦), a [[Euphemism|euphemism]] meaning "comforting, consoling woman." Estimates vary, with most historians placing the number between 20,000 and 200,000, and a significant percentage were minors. After the war, [[Japan]] denied that the system existed. From the 1990s its government offered apologies and compensation, which victims, advocacy groups and scholars have criticized as insincere. Many Japanese officials continue to deny or minimize the system. The government acknowledges that girls and women suffered but disputes that they were taken against their will.

Publication consisting of [[Comics|comics art]] in sequential panels that represent individual scenes.

Panels are often accompanied by prose and dialogue in speech balloons. The first modern American-style comic book, *Famous Funnies: A Carnival of Comics*, was released in 1933 as a reprint of earlier newspaper comic strips. The largest comic book market is Japan, where the [[Manga|manga]] market reached a record ¥612.5 billion in 2020. The comic book market in the United States and Canada was valued at $1.09 billion in 2016. As of 2017 the largest U.S. publisher was the manga distributor Viz Media, followed by [[DC Comics]] and [[Marvel Comics]], whose franchises include [[Superman]], [[Batman]] and [[Spider-Man]].

Form of professional [[Theatre|theater]] originating in Italy and popular across Europe between the 16th and 18th centuries.

Performers played [[Mask|masked]] stock characters identified by name and costume, including the miserly old Pantalone, the clever servant Arlecchino (Harlequin), the know-it-all Il Dottore and the unmasked young lovers, the innamorati. Key plot points and entrances were scripted, but actors [[Improvisational theatre|improvised]] gags and *lazzi* (comic routines) on stage. Troupes such as I Gelosi, whose members included Isabella Andreini, performed in town squares and on platforms. Commedia may be related to [[Carnival]] in [[Venice]], where Andrea Calmo had created the character Il Magnifico by 1570.

Organized system of activities and institutions that facilitate the large-scale exchange of goods, services and other value.

Differences in natural resources and human needs, together with the division of labor, give rise to exchange, and commerce enables specialization and economic interdependence. It traces its origins to barter and periodic marketplaces, and it developed into currency-based trade. Egyptian, Phoenician and Greco-Roman traders expanded commerce along the [[Silk Road]] and through Indian Ocean trade. In medieval times trade hubs such as [[Venice]] connected regions. From the 15th to the early 20th century, European colonial powers dominated global commerce through companies such as the [[Dutch East India Company]] and the [[East India Company|British East India Company]]. The [[Industrial Revolution]] and modern banking reshaped commerce in the 19th century, and standardized shipping containers in the mid-20th century spurred a surge in international trade.

8-bit home computer introduced by Commodore International in January 1982.

It took its name from its 64 kibibytes (65,536 bytes) of RAM and was sold in regular retail stores. It is listed in [[Guinness World Records]] as the best-selling desktop computer model of all time, with independent estimates between 12.5 and 17 million units sold. From 1983 to 1986 it held between 30% and 40% of the U.S. market. It has been compared with the [[Ford Model T]] for bringing new technology to middle-class households. About 10,000 commercial software titles were made for it, including [[Video game|video games]].

[[Roman emperor]] (r. 177–192).

Commodus was nominal co-emperor under his father, [[Marcus Aurelius]], from 177 and ruled alone from 180. In 177, at the age of 16, he became the youngest emperor and consul up to that point. His reign saw less military conflict than his father's, but intrigue and conspiracy led him toward dictatorial rule, including a personality cult and performances as a [[Gladiator|gladiator]] in the [[Colosseum]]. He was assassinated by the wrestler Narcissus, ending the [[Nerva–Antonine dynasty]], and was succeeded by Pertinax, the first claimant in the Year of the Five Emperors.

Calendar notation equivalent to [[Anno Domini|Anno Domini (AD)]] and Before Christ (BC).

"2026 CE" is the same year as "AD 2026," and "400 BCE" the same as "400 BC." The notation avoids religious associations, such as referring to Jesus as *Dominus* ("Lord"). The epoch was devised around 525, and [[Bede]] used it in England in 731. The term "vulgar era" may first appear in a 1615 book by [[Johannes Kepler]]. Use of CE and BCE spread in academic and interfaith settings from the 19th century. Proponents regard it as neutral, while critics contend it preserves the Christian epoch.

Body of law developed chiefly through judicial decisions rather than [[Statute|statutes]].

Under *stare decisis*, courts follow [[Precedent|precedent]] set by earlier decisions, and a judge may establish a new precedent in a case of first impression. The system originated in the practice of the English king's courts after the [[Norman Conquest]] of 1066, unifying law across the kingdom and gradually supplanting local folk and manorial courts. English law spread through the [[British Empire]] to Wales, Ireland and overseas colonies. Many former colonies retain it, and about one-third of the world's population lives in common law or mixed legal systems. *Commentaries on the Laws of England* (1765–1769) by [[William Blackstone]] systematized its principles. The term "judge made law" comes from [[Jeremy Bentham]], who attacked the legitimacy of the common law.

Omnivorous Asian bird of the [[Starling|starling]] family Sturnidae.

The common myna (*Acridotheres tristis*), also called the Indian myna, has adapted well to urban environments and has a strong territorial instinct. [[Carl Linnaeus]] described it in 1766 as *Paradisea tristis*, and its type location was later corrected to Pondicherry in southern India. Two subspecies are recognized. It is brown with a black hooded head, a bare yellow patch behind the eye, and a bright yellow bill and legs. In 2000 the IUCN Species Survival Commission declared it one of the world's most [[Invasive species|invasive species]]. It poses a serious threat to ecosystems in Australia, where it was named "The Most Important Pest/Problem" in 2008.

Small [[Passerine|passerine]] bird in the [[Old World flycatcher]] group, known for its song.

The common nightingale (*Luscinia megarhynchos*) is also called the rufous nightingale. Its song, with whistles, trills and gurgles, is often described as one of the most beautiful sounds in nature. The bird sings at night as well as during the day, which gave it its name, from the Old English *nihtegale* ("night songstress"). Early writers assumed the female sang, but it is the male. It breeds in forest and scrub across Europe and the Palearctic and winters in [[Sub-Saharan Africa]]. In the U.K. numbers fell 53 percent between 1995 and 2008, placing it on the red list. The European population is estimated at 3.2 to 7 million pairs and is classified as least concern.

Flightless bird native to Africa, the largest living bird species.

The common ostrich (*Struthio camelus*) is the tallest and heaviest living bird. Males stand 2.1 to 2.75 m tall and weigh 100 to 130 kg, while females are 1.75 to 1.9 m and weigh 90 to 120 kg. It can run at 55 km/h, with bursts up to about 70 km/h, the fastest land speed of any bipedal animal. It lays the largest eggs of any living bird, although the extinct giant [[Elephant bird|elephant bird]] of [[Madagascar]] and the South Island giant [[Moa|moa]] of New Zealand laid larger ones. Its diet consists mainly of plant matter. It lives in nomadic groups of 5 to 50 birds, and territorial males fight for harems of two to seven females. The species is farmed worldwide for its feathers, skin and meat.

Game bird of the pheasant family Phasianidae, native to Asia.

Also called the ring-necked pheasant, *Phasianus colchicus* takes its species name from Colchis, the region of modern [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] where pheasants became known to Europeans. Its original range extended from the eastern [[Black Sea]] and [[Caspian Sea]] to Manchuria, [[Siberia]], [[Korea]], mainland China and Taiwan. It has been widely introduced as a game bird and is one of the world's most hunted birds. It is also commonly bred on game farms. The ring-necked pheasant is the state bird of [[South Dakota]], one of only two U.S. state birds that is not native to the United States. The green pheasant of [[Japan]] outcompetes the common pheasant, and the introduction of the latter to Japan has largely failed.

Small migratory ground-nesting game bird of the pheasant family Phasianidae.

The common quail (*Coturnix coturnix*) breeds across the Palearctic and winters in Africa and southern India. Its characteristic call is three repeated chirps, and the male's song is a repetitive "wet-my-lips." It is notoriously hard to see, keeping hidden in crops and preferring to creep away rather than fly. Its diet consists of [[Seed|seeds]] and [[Insect|insects]]. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] described it in 1758 as *Tetrao coturnix*. The Japanese quail is now treated as a separate species, since crosses between the two show reduced fertility. Common quails are sometimes kept as [[Poultry|poultry]], and the IUCN classifies the species as least concern.

Large, all-black [[Passerine|passerine]] bird, the most widely distributed [[Corvidae|corvid]].

It is found across the [[Northern Hemisphere]] and is the heaviest passerine bird, averaging 63 cm in length and 1.47 kg. Common ravens can live more than 23 years in the wild. Young birds may travel in flocks, but they later mate for life, with each pair defending a territory. Omnivorous, they feed on carrion, insects, grains, berries, small animals and food waste. Feats of problem-solving show that the species is unusually [[Intelligence|intelligent]]. Many cultures, including Scandinavian, Bhutanese and Siberian, have revered the raven as a spiritual or godlike figure. [[Carl Linnaeus]] first described it in 1758 as *Corvus corax*.

Basic level of knowledge and judgment shared by nearly all people.

The term derives from Latin *sensus communis* and is considered to represent the basic practical judgment that most adults are expected to possess. In philosophy, [[Aristotle]] proposed a *sensus communis* as an inner sense that integrates perceptions from the senses. From the [[Age of Enlightenment|Enlightenment]] onward, the term has been used approvingly, as a standard of good taste and sound judgment, and disapprovingly, as equivalent to conventional wisdom, prejudice and superstition. [[Thomas Paine]]'s pamphlet *Common Sense* (1776) is described as the most influential political pamphlet of the 18th century, affecting the American and French revolutions. The concept remains linked to debates in [[Epistemology|epistemology]] and ethics.

Large freshwater [[Turtle|turtle]] of the family Chelydridae, native to North America.

The common snapping turtle (*Chelydra serpentina*) ranges from [[Canada|southeastern Canada]] to the edge of the [[Rocky Mountains]], east to [[Nova Scotia]] and south to [[Florida]]. Out of water it is combative, with powerful beak-like jaws and a highly mobile head and neck. Northern populations mature at 15 to 20 years, and it usually weighs 4.5 to 16 kg. Males are larger than females, and the heaviest wild specimen caught weighed 34 kg. Long-term mark-recapture data from Algonquin Park in Ontario suggest a maximum age over 100 years. It inhabits shallow [[Pond|ponds]] and streams, often lying beneath muddy bottoms with only its head exposed.

Medium-sized [[Passerine|passerine]] bird of the starling family, native to temperate Europe.

About 20 cm long, it has glossy black plumage with a metallic sheen, speckled with white in some seasons. Its gift for mimicry was noted by [[Pliny the Elder]] and [[William Shakespeare]]. It nests in a natural or artificial cavity, where four or five glossy, pale blue eggs are laid. The species is omnivorous, eating invertebrates, seeds and fruit. Large flocks can help control agricultural pests, but they also damage fruit and sprouting crops. It has been introduced as an invasive species to Australia, New Zealand, [[North America]], Mexico, Argentina, South Africa and Fiji. Its numbers have declined in northern and western Europe since the 1980s, but it is classified as least concern by the IUCN.

Large annual forb in the daisy family [[Asteraceae]].

The most common varieties have large yellow-orange flower heads on a tall stem. The domesticated form is harvested for edible seeds, which are used for oil or confectionery. Oilseed sunflowers are the fourth most used [[Vegetable oil|vegetable oil]] in the world, while confectionery seeds are eaten as a [[Snack|snack]]. Production is concentrated in [[Ukraine]], Russia and the European Union. Seeds in the flower head follow the [[Fibonacci sequence]]. Mature flower heads point in a fixed, typically easterly direction rather than tracking the Sun, a misconception that John Gerard disputed in 1597. The tallest recorded specimen was 10.9 m.

Cultivated [[Wheat|wheat]] species, also known as bread wheat.

It originated around 8,000 years ago from the hybridization of an already domesticated wheat with wild goatgrass in the South Caucasus or southwestern Caspian area. About 95% of the wheat produced worldwide is this species, making it the most widely grown of all crops and the [[Cereal|cereal]] with the highest monetary yield. Bread wheat is an allohexaploid, with four sets of chromosomes from emmer and two from *Aegilops tauschii*, which gives it greater cold hardiness. Modern varieties carry dwarfing genes that [[Norman Borlaug]] introduced in the 1960s from Norin 10 wheat grown in [[Japan]], shortening stems to prevent lodging. Bread wheat has displaced many [[Barley]] and [[Rye]] species once used for bread, particularly in Europe.

Eurasian intergovernmental organization formed after the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]].

Belarus, [[Russia]] and [[Ukraine]] signed the Belovezha Accords on December 8, 1991, declaring that the Union had ceased to exist and establishing the CIS in its place. On December 21, eight more former Soviet republics signed the Alma-Ata Protocol. [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] joined in 1993 and withdrew in 2008 after a war with Russia. Ukraine stopped participating after Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea. [[Moldova]] denounced the CIS treaty, protocol and charter on April 8, 2026, after beginning to withdraw following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Eight of the nine member states participate in the CIS Free Trade Area, and three organizations originated from it, including the Eurasian Economic Union.

International association of 56 member states, most of them former territories of the [[British Empire]].

Members share use of the [[English language|English language]] and cultural and historical ties. The Commonwealth Secretariat handles intergovernmental relations, and the Commonwealth Foundation handles nongovernmental ones. The association was defined as the British Commonwealth of Nations in the 1926 Balfour Declaration, and the 1949 London Declaration allowed [[India]] to remain a member as a republic. Member states have no legal obligations to one another, though the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is the supreme court of 14 countries. The Commonwealth Charter defines shared values of [[Democracy|democracy]], [[Human rights|human rights]] and the [[Rule of law|rule of law]]. [[Charles III]] is head of the Commonwealth, succeeding his mother, [[Elizabeth II]]. He is king of 15 member states, while 36 are republics and five have other monarchs.
